item.title: Mid-mantle discontinuities beneath subduction zones linked to depth-dependent deformation of bridgmanite
item.dc:creator: John Keith Magali
Sébastien Merkel

item.description: Abstract Bridgmanite, the main mineralogical phase in the Earth’s lower mantle, is intrinsically anisotropic and may therefore generate seismic anisotropy in actively-deforming regions, particularly subduction zones. The bulk of the lower mantle is widely regarded as well-mixed but recent seismic observations suggest structures at mid-mantle depths whose origin remains unclear. Here, we propose a mechanism that could generate seismic discontinuities beneath subduction zones with depth distributions consistent with some of the observed mid-mantle reflectors. By coupling thermo-mechanical subduction models with pressure-dependent fabric calculations, we show that gradual slip transitions in bridgmanite with depth can manifest anisotropic discontinuities near 1000 km, which can deepen depending on the extent of accumulated deformation. This discontinuity is most pronounced in regions of strong slab-driven flow as revealed by its reflection coefficients, the strength of which varies with distance and azimuth. While our models predict ~ 1.5% contrast in fast versus slow shear wave velocities in terms of radial anisotropy, our full waveform simulations show that the discontinuity is detectable with array seismological methods. These results suggest that mid-mantle reflectors near subduction zones may be strain-induced, providing an additional mechanism that links mantle flow, mineral physics, and seismic observations. item.description: Divergent models persist for the emergence of animals. Lipid biomarkers suggest animals originated before 635 million years ago (Ma), but their body fossil record extends to only 574 Ma. item.description: Deep-sea holobionts adapt to extreme environmental fluctuations, but the molecular mechanisms underlying resilience remain poorly understood. We investigated the vesicomyid clam Archivesica marissinica and its sulfur-oxidizing symbionts during sulfide shortage via in situ transplant experiments at the Haima cold seep. Transplanting clams to sulfide-depleted conditions (moderate at HM-3 and severe at HM-2) revealed distinct response patterns of host-symbiont interaction. Symbionts may mitigate sulfide loss by shifting from sulfide oxidation to thiosulfate oxidation, supported by thiosulfate generated through host sulfide detoxification pathways. Notably, symbiont abundance remained stable under moderate sulfide shortage (HM-3), accompanied by down-regulation of host endosomal maturation and fusion with lysosomes, potentially limiting symbiont turnover. Conversely, severe sulfide shortage (HM-2) was associated with up-regulation of lysosomal pathways and lower symbiont abundance. These results demonstrate tiered molecular adaptations—metabolic flexibility and shifts in symbiont dynamics—enabling holobiont resilience to spatially heterogeneous sulfide availability in deep-sea seeps, supporting ecosystem stability. item.title: Deep learning of fossil pollen morphology reveals 25,000 y of ecological change in eastern African grasslands
item.dc:creator: Marc-Élie Adaimé

item.prism:publicationName: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
item.description: Grass (Poaceae) pollen is largely overlooked in investigations of grassland evolution because the pollen of most species cannot be differentiated using traditional optical microscopy. However, the combination of superresolution microscopy and deep learning enables the capture and quantification of distinct morphological variation across the pollen of grass species. Using a semisupervised deep-learning strategy, we trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on superresolution images of known modern and unlabeled fossil grass pollen. We used learned CNN features to estimate taxonomic diversity and discriminate between C 3 and C 4 grass species—applying Shannon entropy as a measure of morphological variability and a gradient-boosted decision tree as a classifier of photosynthetic type. We validated the method on modern grass pollen assemblages and then applied our trained models to fossil assemblages from a 25,000-y lake-sediment record from Mt. Kenya, correlating shifts in grass diversity through time with changes in atmospheric CO 2 concentration and proxy records of local temperature, precipitation, and fire occurrence. Our data show that the species diversity of these montane grasslands declined substantially between 21,500 and 16,000 years ago, coincident with the most severe regional cooling of the last ice age, and that the fraction of C 4 grasses gradually decreased after the late-glacial–Holocene transition, associated with higher temperatures and decreasing fire activity. Our results demonstrate that CNN features of pollen morphology can advance palynological analysis and enable robust estimation of changes in grass diversity and C 4 grass abundance in ancient grassland ecosystems. item.description: Although increasing evidence implicates subchondral bone alterations in osteoarthritis, the spatial organization of subchondral bone remodeling remains unclear. Applying spatial transcriptomics to human subchondral bone, we identify a spatially conserved osteogenic core-halo architecture that displays transcriptional reprogramming in sclerotic microenvironments. Spatial dependency and a customized cell-cell communication framework reveal disrupted osteoblast-osteoclast spatial coupling, enhanced osteoblast-mesenchymal interactions, and identify FN1-SDC2 and COL1A1-DDR2 as candidate stromal-osteogenic signaling axes that may contribute to aberrant bone remodeling. Additionally, we present the in situ transcriptional landscape of osteocytes and reveal its potential regulatory role in aberrant bone remodeling. We further delineate a continuum of spatial ecotypes exhibiting distinct enrichment, spatial topology reorganization, and inter-ecotype communication rewiring across pathological states. Metabolic flux inference additionally reveals substrate-limited, stressed states across multiple ecotypes in sclerotic microenvironments. Collectively, our findings provide critical insights into aberrant subchondral bone remodeling in osteoarthritis and offer a valuable framework for future mechanistic studies and therapeutic exploration. Subchondral bone remodeling is increasingly implicated in osteoarthritis, but its spatial organization remain incompletely understood. This study provides a high-resolution spatial map of subchondral bone and identifies conserved spatial architectures, revealing distinct microenvironmental states and candidate signaling pathways associated with subchondral bone sclerosis. item.description: Coupled Sb-Hg isotope signatures from the South China antimony belt reveal that ore metals were sourced from both Precambrian basement rocks and a deep recycled mantle reservoir, demonstrating the utility of coupled Sb-Hg isotopes for tracing metal provenance, according to coupled Sb and Hg isotope analyses. Understanding the sources of metals in hydrothermal ore systems is fundamental for improving exploration models. However, direct tracers of metal sources remain limited, especially for large, low-temperature deposits. Here we apply coupled antimony (Sb) and mercury (Hg) isotope analyses to Sb deposits from South China, the World’s largest antimony metallogenic province. The dataset reveals substantial variability in δ^123Sb (−0.64 to +0.69‰), δ^202Hg (−1.86 to +2.08‰), and Δ^199Hg (−0.20 to +0.14‰). These data support a model involving two metal sources, namely a deep, recycled mantle-related reservoir and Precambrian basement metamorphic rocks. Our results demonstrate that coupled Sb and Hg isotopes provide a potentially powerful tool with which to identify the metal sources for Sb ore deposits, and that their application may help refine models for these deposits globally and help decode the dynamic interplay between Earth’s interior and crustal metal cycling. item.description: Abstract Reactive iron oxide-bound organic carbon (Fe–OC) is a key pathway for long-term carbon burial, but its effectiveness under increasingly widespread eutrophication remains uncertain. item.title: Snowball refrigeration of Earth’s crust mimics glacial erosion
item.dc:creator: R. M. Flowers
F. A. Macdonald
R. S. Anderson
item.description: Glaciation cools the crust by setting its surface temperature to 0°C or well below. During the Cryogenian Snowball Earth glaciations, these conditions were in place long enough to cool the entire crustal column. Although crustal thermal history can be deciphered by thermochronology, these data are typically interpreted to record depth changes due to burial or erosion. Thermal models of the crust under Cryogenian boundary conditions predict that thermochronometers were substantially altered in the upper quarter to half of the crust. This Snowball Earth refrigeration, with little to no coeval erosion, may have imparted a cooling signal mimicking up to 3‒5 km of glacial erosion. Rock cooling previously attributed to massive Snowball erosion and linked to the Great Unconformity may instead reflect a great refrigeration of Earth’s crust, with implications for thermochronology across other climate events. item.description: True polar wander (TPW) is presently occurring at a rate of ~10 centimeters per year, exceeding the mean rate of differential plate motion. Whether this rate is transient and negligible on geological timescales or whether Earth has experienced rapid TPW lasting millions of years is unclear. Paleomagnetic evidence has been used to propose fast episodes of TPW, but limitations of the paleomagnetic record have precluded definitive results. Rapid TPW will induce global sea level fluctuations associated with relative changes in centrifugal potential, offering an independent test. We evaluated this prediction using continental flooding reconstructions and identified multiple robust quadrupolar patterns since 320 million years ago, confirming that protracted rapid TPW has occurred on Earth and that couplings among Earth’s rotational dynamics, mantle processes, and surface environments can be strongly episodic. item.description: Abstract The subduction of crustal rocks to, and exhumation from, depths greater than 90 km in the stability field of the mineral coesite is known as ultrahigh-pressure metamorphism, widely regarded as evidence for cold subduction. This assumption stems from peak metamorphic conditions of ultrahigh-pressure rocks, which indicate low subduction gradients of less than 330 °C GPa −1 , but direct evidence for such a cold prograde evolution is lacking. Here we report the discovery of a young ultrahigh-pressure eclogite in eastern Papua New Guinea. We find (sub)micrometre-sized inclusions of coesite in intermediate growth zones of garnet crystals and zircon inclusions revealing a U–Pb age of approximately 4.4 million years. Petrographic observations and thermo-barometric methods show that the prograde subduction path was initially warm with an apparent average gradient of approximately 470 °C GPa −1 until a depth of about 45 km, before switching to a cold thermal regime with ultrafast subduction rates of greater than 60 mm yr −1 (vertical component). This change in geothermal gradients can be explained by shear heating and/or by formation during the non-steady-state phase of a young subduction zone. We propose that high geothermal gradients at shallow levels of deep subduction systems might be common, challenging the use of peak metamorphic conditions as indicator for subduction zone thermal structures. item.description: Abstract Urban land subsidence driven by groundwater extraction is widespread, but the processes governing how groundwater recovery translates into spatially variable surface uplift remain poorly understood. item.dc:creator: Bowen Hou

item.description: The viral contributions to deep-sea polymetallic ecosystems, rich in valuable mineral nodules, remain unclear. Here, the authors created the first large-scale catalog of viruses from the Clarion-Clipperton Fracture Zone and found extensive viral diversity that may influence nutrient cycling, microbial survival, and adaptation to metal-rich environments. Deep-sea polymetallic nodule provinces host distinct benthic prokaryotic communities, yet viruses that regulate them remain largely unknown. Here, we established the viral genome dataset of the Clarion-Clipperton Fracture Zone, the world’s largest deep-sea mineral exploration region, to investigate viral diversity and ecological functions. Protein-sharing network and phylogenetic analyses showed extensive benthic viral diversity, with over 99% of viral clusters not represented in current reference databases. Inferred virus–host associations suggest that viral infections span a broad range of prokaryotic lineages involved in carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur, and metal cycling. By infecting key functional microbes and encoding auxiliary metabolic genes, viruses may modulate host metabolism and survival during infection, with potential implications for biogeochemical processes in polymetallic nodule field sediments. Moreover, gene exchange analyses indicate the potential of viruses to facilitate host adaptation to metal stress. These findings provide insights into the ecological roles of viruses in the polymetallic nodule province, establishing a vital pre-mining baseline of microbial ecosystem for future environmental impact assessments. item.description: Recent studies show that subduction zones host both biogenic and abiotic organic carbon. The latter can form under high-pressure and high-temperature conditions, yet the mechanisms and redox controls remain poorly constrained. We present piston-cylinder experiments at 700 °C and 3 GPa simulating carbonate reduction in the presence of antigorite over a wide oxygen fugacity range, from about ΔFMQ −4 to −1 relative to fayalite–magnetite–quartz (FMQ) buffer. Graphitic carbon forms under all investigated redox conditions, and is systematically associated with chlorite derived from antigorite breakdown. Raman spectroscopy, TOF- and Orbi- SIMS analyses indicate that under the most reducing conditions investigated i.e., approaching those imposed by wüstite–magnetite buffer (ΔFMQ ≈ −4), abundant graphitic carbon forms and is highly ordered, hydrogen-poor and dominated by aromatic structures. In contrast, less reducing conditions (buffered at nickel–nickel oxide, ΔFMQ ≈ −1), yield smaller amounts of highly disordered, partially hydrogenated and oxygenated graphitic carbon. These differences, observed under identical pressure and temperature, primarily reflects the influence of oxygen fugacity, indicating a redox-driven formation pathway distinct from the thermal maturation and graphitization of biogenic organic matter. Such redox-driven precipitation of graphitic carbon may promote transient carbon storage, facilitate volatile transport into the deep mantle and contribute to the diversity of metastable carbon species involved in the deep carbon cycling. item.description: The metasomatized subcontinental lithospheric mantle (SCLM) is widely recognized as a major source for the formation of giant gold deposits. However, it remains debated whether the Triassic subduction of the Yangtze plate or the Jurassic subduction of the Paleo-Pacific plate beneath the eastern North China Craton (NCC) contributed more significantly to the Au budget of the Jiaodong gold province. This study presents petrological and geochronological (zircon and apatite U-Pb) data for the Jinshan lamprophyres, identifying Late Jurassic (ca. 155–152 Ma) vogesite and Early Cretaceous (ca. 139 Ma) odinite. Both types exhibit typical island-arc basalt (IAB)-like geochemical characteristics, including enrichment in large ion lithophile elements (LILEs) and light rare earth elements (LREEs), depletion in high field strength elements (HFSEs) and heavy rare earth elements (HREEs), and low abundances and fractionated patterns of platinum-group elements (PGEs), similar to those of regional Early Cretaceous IAB-type mafic rocks. Key geochemical evidence indicates a pyroxenite-rich, amphibole-bearing mantle as the source. The parental magmas of the Jinshan lamprophyres were derived from low-degree (~4%) partial melting of the mantle source within the spinel–garnet transition zone. However, they exhibit more enriched Sr-Nd-Pb isotopic signatures than the regional Early Cretaceous mafic rocks. Their isotopic similarity to coeval lamprophyres in eastern Liaodong and mafic rocks from the South China Block (SCB) suggests that the mantle source was significantly modified by Paleo-Pacific slab-derived metasomatism. In contrast, the isotopic signatures of the regional Early Cretaceous mafic rocks are more akin to those of the Sulu–Dabie orogen, implying a significant contribution from the Yangtze plate. The systematic depletion and fractionation of PGEs in the Jinshan lamprophyres indicate that these features were inherited from low-degree mantle melting and not produced by shallow crustal processes. The Au content of the Jinshan lamprophyres (~0.096 ppb) is higher than that of the ancient NCC SCLM (~0.085 ppb) but lower than that of the Sulu orogenic peridotites (~0.355 ppb) and that of the syn-mineralization Early Cretaceous mafic rocks (~1.35 ppb). Integrated with previous studies, the data presented here suggest that Yangtze-derived materials may have contributed more significantly to mantle Au fertility, whereas Paleo-Pacific metasomatism primarily enhanced the volatile–fluid conditions conducive to Au mobilization. Furthermore, the Early Cretaceous mafic rocks coeval with large-scale gold mineralization exhibit Au concentrations (~1.35 ppb) comparable to those of global metasomatized lithospheric mantle (~1–1.2 ppb). This implies that the extensive Early Cretaceous gold mineralization in the Jiaodong Peninsula did not require a pre-enriched mantle source but instead was controlled by favorable conditions for Au release and transport induced by Paleo-Pacific plate subduction. item.description: The metasomatized lithospheric mantle has been proposed as the primary source for gold mineralization at cratonic margins, yet without much direct evidence. To substantiate this theory with geochemistry, we study ore-hosting alkaline syenite and mineralization-related lamprophyre dikes from the Huangtuliang gold deposit at the northern margin of the North China Craton. We provide new zircon U-Pb geochronology and Hf isotope data, as well as whole-rock major and trace element analyses. The alkaline syenite was emplaced during the Early Devonian (397 ± 1 Ma), while the lamprophyre magmatism and associated gold mineralization occurred in the Late Jurassic (152 ± 1 Ma). The alkaline syenite is characterized by high K2O (10.4–10.9 wt%; loss-on-ignition–free) contents and K2O/Na2O (4.0–4.3) ratios, as well as negative zircon εHf(t) values (−22.5 to −18.2). Its formation is interpreted to have involved (1) low-degree partial melting of a phlogopite-rich lithospheric mantle potentially metasomatized by subduction-derived fluids and carbonatitic melts and (2) fractional crystallization during magma ascent. The lamprophyre dikes exhibit high K2O (2.19–4.17 wt%) and TiO2 (2.98–3.22 wt%) contents and positive zircon εHf(t) values (+3.1 to +8.2), suggesting their parent magma likely originated from a metasomatized, garnet-bearing asthenospheric mantle source and evolved through fractional crystallization. item.description: Fe-rich carbonates (siderite and ankerite) of banded iron formations (BIF) are considered as a potential carbon source to produce diamonds during subduction in Mesoarchean to Paleoproterozoic. Here, we experimentally demonstrate that diamond nucleation and subsequent growth can occur via the interaction of siderite, originated from subducted BIFs, with sulfur-rich mantle fluids under pressure of 6.3 GPa and temperatures of 1450–1550 °C, corresponding to Archean subduction geotherm. Under these conditions, Fe,Ca,Mg-carbonate melt with dissolved sulfur can probably act as both diamond formation medium and carbon source, and the driving forces for diamond growth might be the redox reactions of carbonate and sulfide melts. Resulting diamonds are predominantly octahedral, contain 300–900 ppm nitrogen, host sulfide, graphite, carbonate and magnetite inclusions and display new vibronic systems with zero-phonon lines at 429 and 693 nm, which are most likely associated with S- and Fe-related defects in the diamond lattice. We demonstrate that diamond growth rate and the number of inclusions increases with increasing iron content of the carbonate melt with dissolved sulfur. These features provide diagnostic criteria for natural diamonds with magnetite inclusions and specific defect-impurity characteristics. We developed a model of Precambrian diamond formation in subducted carbonated BIFs, that consists of the sequential implementation of processes: (1) sulfidation of siderite, (2) siderite partial decomposition with magnetite +C0 + O2/CO2 formation, and (3) diamond-producing redox interactions between Fe,Mg,Ca,Mn-carbonate melt and sulfide melt. item.description: Gold mineralization in Precambrian high-grade metamorphic terranes, particularly those hosted within middle- to lower-crustal upper amphibolite- to granulite-facies domains, remains a metallogenic paradox. item.description: Granite-related Sn–W polymetallic deposits represent a major global source of Sn and W, yet the mechanisms driving their co-enrichment with chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu, Ag) remain poorly understood. Based on ages and metal associations, the ore-related intrusions are classified into four groups: (1) Sn–W-related Cretaceous peraluminous granites; (2) Ag-related Cretaceous metaluminous to weakly peraluminous granites; (3) Sn–W–Cu-related Early Paleozoic mafic–granitic rocks; and (4) Sn–Cu-related Cretaceous mafic–granitic rocks. These granite types display distinct elemental and isotopic signatures, reflecting diverse origins and evolutionary processes: (1) Sn–W-related granites formed via mica (muscovite and biotite)-dehydration melting of Proterozoic metapelites; (2) Ag-related granites derived from amphibole-dehydration melting of Proterozoic amphibolites; (3) Sn–W–Cu-related granites originated from mica-dehydration melting of Proterozoic metapelites with additional input from asthenospheric mantle-derived mafic magmas; and (4) Sn–Cu-related granites stemmed from a similar metapelitic source but with contributions from enriched lithospheric mantle-derived mafic magmas. These two systems, coupled via the injection of mafic magmas into metapelite-derived granitic magmas, control the co-enrichment of Sn–W and chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu) within a single deposit. These magmatic–metallogenic frameworks demonstrate the role of a three-tiered cascading model—ranging from crustal sources (metapelites vs. amphibolites), through melting mechanisms (muscovite-, biotite-, and amphibole-dehydration melting), to mantle inputs (enriched lithospheric vs. asthenospheric mantle)—in controlling the co-enrichment of Sn–W and chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu). This cascading model is governed by first-order geodynamic triggers, including polyphase tectonic evolution and unique geodynamic mechanisms. Based on these considerations, we define three diagnostic criteria—petrological, elemental, and isotopic—that can effectively distinguish Sn–W–Cu systems from Sn–W-only systems. Thus, this work greatly advances our understanding of metallogenic specialization in granitic systems, and holds significant implications for exploring diverse Sn–W polymetallic deposits in analogous settings worldwide. It exhibits a progressive lithological transition from amazonite-free granite in the lower lithological zones (LLZ) to amazonite-rich granite and pegmatite veins in the middle lithological zones (MLZ) to amazonite-poor granite in the upper lithological zone (ULZ), which formed as a result of the magmatic–hydrothermal evolution of a single granitic melt. Accordingly, this pluton provides a unique opportunity to investigate the mechanisms of rare metal mineralization through quantitatively constraining the origin and physicochemical properties of fluids, and by evaluating how these fluids drive geochemical fractionation during magmatic–hydrothermal evolution. item.description: Peridotite xenoliths from the Tariat region of Mongolia are representative of the MORB-source mantle in terms of trace element patterns and radiogenic isotopic ratios, with rare metasomatic enrichments. item.description: The base of cratonic lithospheric mantle (cratonic root) is a key volatile-rich reservoir (e.g., carbon and halogens), formed through long-term metasomatism by deep-derived incipient melts, whose reactivation has been proposed to drive climatic change over the course of Earth history. item.description: Mantle sections in ophiolites are almost always serpentinized. In contrast, trace elements (e.g., Sc, Ti, V, Mn, Co, Ni, Zn, and Ga) exhibit relatively homogeneous distributions and provide more robust insights into parental magma composition and crustal assimilation processes. item.description: The Jiangnan Orogen is the world's largest Au-Sb-W metallogenic belt and an ideal natural laboratory for investigating polymetallic mineralization. Its pronounced positive Eu anomaly suggests precipitation under highly reducing conditions, whereas its stable association with ankerite indicates a neutral to weakly alkaline fluid environment. These conditions were probably favored by structurally controlled fluid ascent along NWW-trending faults. Pressure decrease during this process may have promoted local phase separation, CO₂ escape, and pH increase, thereby providing a plausible mechanism for efficient Sch-1a precipitation under reducing, neutral to weakly alkaline conditions. item.description: Subducting slabs in the mantle transition zone (MTZ) exhibit complex deformation patterns and host deep-focus earthquakes. Two long-standing puzzles concern why some slabs stagnate near the 660-km discontinuity while others penetrate into the lower mantle, and how earthquake-like failure can occur under the high-pressure conditions of the deep mantle. A key process linking these phenomena is the metastable transformation of olivine to its high-pressure polymorphs within cold slab interiors. Kinetic inhibition of this transition can lead to the formation of a metastable olivine wedge (MOW), which modifies slab buoyancy, releases latent heat, and produces fine-grained microstructures. Laboratory experiments and seismic observations provide strong evidence for the existence of MOWs, yet the dynamic consequences of the buoyancy and grain-size changes on slab morphology, kinematics, and long-term evolution have not been explored in self-consistent dynamic models. Here we show that incorporating fully coupled metastable kinetics with both grain-boundary nucleation and interface-controlled grain growth, together with grain-size–dependent composite rheology, fundamentally alters subduction dynamics in both 2-D and 3-D free-subduction models. When transition kinetics reduce grain size within the slab interior, our simulations predict that the MOW persistently extends deeper than 550 km for an 80 Ma slab. The resulting time-dependent buoyancy suppresses slab folding above the MOW by buffering subducting-plate velocities, whereas the small grain size promotes folding below the MOW through rheological weakening. In addition, models with both a MOW and grain-size evolution strongly promote trench retreat and the development of trench curvature. Together, these results demonstrate that metastable kinetics and grain-size evolution provide a unifying framework for linking microscopic phase-transition processes to macroscopic slab dynamics, offering new insight into slab morphology and the physical conditions governing deep-focus earthquakes.
